# Genesis 26 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Structure & Overview

The chapter can be divided into five sections: the covenant reaffirmed to Isaac (vv. 1–6), the wife–sister deception (vv. 7–11), prosperity and conflict over wells (vv. 12–22), God's appearance at Beersheba and covenant with Abimelech (vv. 23–33), and Esau's Hittite marriages (vv. 34–35). Nearly every commentator notes that this is the only chapter devoted exclusively to Isaac, and that his experiences deliberately parallel those of Abraham—famine, covenant, deception before Abimelech, well disputes, and a peace treaty.

---

## v. 1 — The Famine and Journey to Gerar

**Traditional reading:** This famine was distinct from the one in Abraham's day (Genesis 12:10), occurring about a century later. Isaac, who had been living at Lahai-roi near Beersheba (cf. Genesis 25:11), began moving southward toward Egypt along the Mediterranean coastal route, stopping at Gerar — the same Philistine city where Abraham had once sojourned.

- **Gill** notes that "Abimelech" was likely a dynastic title (like "Pharaoh"), not the same individual Abraham dealt with, and that Isaac came "from Lahairoi, where he had dwelt many years … about eight miles from Gerar." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/26.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary** estimates 70–80 years had elapsed since Abraham's stay; "it is scarcely probable that this was the monarch who then reigned." — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/26.htm
- **JFB** says the pressure of famine forced Isaac "with his family and flocks to migrate into the land of the Philistines, where he was exposed to personal danger, as his father had been." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/genesis/26.htm
- **Guzik (Enduring Word)** observes that living in the land of promise did not mean life would be "without trouble or challenge." Isaac seems to have intended to go all the way to Egypt, as Abraham did. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-26/

**Reformed perspective:** Calvin viewed this as a test of Isaac's faith and dependence on God's providence. God permitted the famine to try him and then intervened to prevent him from fleeing the promised land. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/genesis-26.html

---

## vv. 2–5 — God Appears and Reaffirms the Covenant

**Traditional reading:** The LORD (Yahweh, the covenant God) appeared to Isaac — one of only two recorded theophanies to him (the other in v. 24). God forbade him to go to Egypt, commanded him to dwell in the land God would show him, and formally transferred the Abrahamic covenant to Isaac with its three core promises: land, innumerable descendants, and universal blessing through his "seed."

- **Gill:** God's prohibition was "partly to try his faith … and partly lest he should think of continuing there, and be unmindful of the promise of the land of Canaan to Abraham's seed." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/26.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary** suggests this appearance may have occurred at Lahai-roi before Isaac reached Gerar, and that it was the cause of Isaac's turning aside into Philistia rather than continuing to Egypt (contra Keil, Lange, Murphy who place it in Gerar). — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/26.htm
- **Guzik:** This was "a significant appearance" — "The Son of Promise was always to live in the land of promise." He notes the three essential covenant aspects: land, nation, and blessing. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-26/
- **Bible.org (Bob Deffinbaugh):** "For him this was no dull recital but a thrilling assurance that what God had promised Abraham, He now promised his son. This is a covenant with Isaac." — https://bible.org/seriespage/isaac-walks-his-father%E2%80%99s-steps-genesis-261-35
- **JFB** connects v. 2 to Psalm 105:14–15, seeing divine preservation at work. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/genesis/26.htm

### v. 4 — "through your offspring all nations … will be blessed"

**Traditional reading:** This is a direct messianic promise. The "seed" (offspring) ultimately points to Christ (Galatians 3:16).

- **Gill:** "Meaning in the Messiah that should spring from him, see Genesis 22:18." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/26.htm
- **Guzik:** This is the third essential aspect of the Abrahamic covenant repeated. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-26/

All major Protestant traditions agree this is a messianic prophecy fulfilled in Jesus Christ.

### v. 5 — "Because Abraham obeyed My voice and kept My charge, My commandments, My statutes, and My laws"

**Traditional reading:** This verse is notable for using Mosaic-era legal terminology (charge, commandments, statutes, laws) to describe Abraham's obedience long before the Law was given. Commentators draw several implications:

- **Bible.org:** "By the use of these terms Moses … indicates that 'laws, commandments, charges, and statutes' are nothing new but were involved already in patriarchal religion." — https://bible.org/seriespage/isaac-walks-his-father%E2%80%99s-steps-genesis-261-35
- **Guzik:** "God kept the covenant with Isaac because of Abraham's obedience. A close look at Abraham's life shows that his obedience wasn't complete or constant; yet God recognized it." He adds that "Abraham was declared righteous by faith (Genesis 15:6). The righteousness accounted to Abraham was the righteousness of God Himself." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-26/
- **Gill:** God's words are "mentioned rather as an example to Isaac, and to stir him up to do the like, as if it was said, because or seeing that Abraham thy father did so and so, do thou likewise." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/26.htm

**Reformed (Calvin/Ligonier):** The obedience of Abraham is seen as evidence of his faith, not meritorious ground of the covenant. The covenant rests on God's sovereign grace; Abraham's obedience demonstrates the fruit of that grace. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/promise-isaac-part

**Methodist/Wesleyan:** This verse is sometimes cited to show that genuine faith expresses itself in obedient keeping of God's commands — faith and obedience are not opposed but intertwined. Abraham's obedience is the pattern for covenant faithfulness.

---

## vv. 6–7 — Isaac's Deception

**Traditional reading:** Isaac obeyed by staying in Gerar (v. 6), but when the men of the place inquired about Rebekah, he lied, calling her his sister. This is the third occurrence of the wife–sister deception in Genesis (cf. 12:10–20; 20:1–18). Isaac's lie was worse than Abraham's because Rebekah was not actually his sister, even as a half-truth.

- **Gill:** "Herein imitating his father Abraham in his infirmity and unbelief … though cousins might be called sisters, yet this was mere dissimulation … and therefore not justifiable." He notes Rebekah was still beautiful "though she had been married in all probability forty years or more." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/26.htm
- **Guzik:** "Isaac went from the a high spiritual experience of receiving the explicit promise of the covenant … to this obvious sin because of his failure to trust God's protection." He notes Isaac's lie "didn't even have the advantage of being a half-truth" and "made Rebekah more vulnerable and in greater danger." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-26/
- **Bible.org:** "Frightened concerning his own safety, Isaac succumbs to the temptation … In doing this he was willing to risk Rebekah's purity as the price for his personal protection." — https://bible.org/seriespage/isaac-walks-his-father%E2%80%99s-steps-genesis-261-35
- **JFB:** Isaac "was exposed to personal danger, as his father had been on account of his wife's beauty; but through the seasonable interposition of Providence, he was preserved." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/genesis/26.htm

**Reformed (Ligonier):** "Isaac's timidity was his greatest weakness here, and it led to his reprimand from Abimelech." — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/promise-isaac-part

**Generational sin observation:** Guzik notes that "the Bible doesn't teach we are bound by what are sometimes known as generational curses, but it is often the case that the sins of the fathers are found in the children" because they are "nurtured in the same environment and patterned by a previous generation." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-26/

---

## vv. 8–11 — Discovery and Rebuke by Abimelech

**Traditional reading:** After a "long time" (perhaps years), Abimelech happened to look through a window and saw Isaac "caressing" (KJV: "sporting with") Rebekah in a manner obviously appropriate for a wife, not a sister. The pagan king rebuked Isaac, warning that someone could have unwittingly committed adultery — which Abimelech regarded as bringing "guilt" on his people. He then issued a death-penalty decree protecting Isaac and Rebekah.

- **Gill:** Abimelech observed Isaac's behaviour "accidentally, and not out of curiosity." The word "lightly" (v. 10) in the Hebrew can mean "within a little" — implying it was nearly too late. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/26.htm
- **Guzik:** "What Isaac thought could be hidden was obvious to others. This is often the case with sin among God's people." God protected Isaac and Rebekah "even though Isaac put his wife in danger and trusted in his ability to deceive more than in God's ability to protect." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-26/
- **Bible.org:** "Abimelech's ethics appear to be based on a higher standard than Isaac's … Abimelech seemed to regard marital purity higher than Isaac did." — https://bible.org/seriespage/isaac-walks-his-father%E2%80%99s-steps-genesis-261-35
- **Pulpit Commentary** notes the contrast with Genesis 20 where God directly threatened Abimelech in a dream; here Abimelech discerns the truth through natural observation. — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/26.htm

---

## vv. 12–14 — The Hundredfold Blessing and Envy

**Traditional reading:** Isaac sowed seed (farming, not just herding) and reaped a hundredfold in the same year — an exceptional yield. He grew progressively wealthy in flocks, herds, and servants, prompting Philistine envy.

- **Gill:** Cites Pliny and Herodotus on extraordinary crop yields in antiquity (150-fold in Byzacium, 200–300 fold near Nineveh), demonstrating this was remarkable but not unbelievable. "The Lord blessed him; and prospered and succeeded all his endeavours; and this was the true reason of the fertility." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/26.htm
- **JFB:** "During his sojourn in that district he farmed a piece of land, which, by the blessing of God on his skill and industry, was very productive … and by his plentiful returns he increased so rapidly in wealth and influence that the Philistines, afraid or envious of his prosperity, obliged him to leave." Notes parallels in modern Syria where shepherds settle temporarily and are forced out by jealous landowners. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/genesis/26.htm
- **Guzik:** "Prosperity came to Isaac as the blessing upon his hard work. He probably received enough of an inheritance from his father that he did not have to labor, but worked hard nonetheless, and God blessed it." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-26/
- **Bible.org:** "In spite of Isaac's deception, God poured out His blessings upon him." — https://bible.org/seriespage/isaac-walks-his-father%E2%80%99s-steps-genesis-261-35

**Word of Faith / Prosperity teaching:** Some prosperity-gospel teachers cite the "hundredfold" return in v. 12 as a "law of sowing and reaping" promising financial hundredfold returns to believers who give generously. This chapter is a key proof-text in that tradition. *However, none of the trusted commentary sources consulted (Gill, JFB, Guzik, Pulpit, Calvin, Bible.org) interpret this as a universal promise of financial prosperity; they treat it as a specific, historical blessing on Isaac within God's covenant purposes.* The traditional reading emphasises that the blessing was God's sovereign gift, not an automatic mechanism, and came alongside trials (envy, well-stopping, expulsion).

**Reformed (Ligonier):** "Whenever the Lord grants us great success, we should not be surprised if people envy us. Opposition will often come from non-believers, but unfortunately, other Christians may become jealous too (Num. 12)." — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/promise-isaac-part

---

## vv. 15–17 — Wells Stopped Up; Expulsion from Gerar

**Traditional reading:** The Philistines, out of envy, filled Abraham's old wells with earth — an act of economic warfare since wells were precious, expensive assets in an arid land. Abimelech then asked Isaac to leave, saying he was "much mightier than we."

- **Gill:** The Philistines "durst not stop [the wells] during his [Abraham's] life; but when he was dead and particularly out of envy to Isaac his son … they stopped them up." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/26.htm
- **JFB:** "The same base stratagem for annoying those against whom they have taken an umbrage is practiced still by choking the wells with sand or stones, or defiling them with putrid carcases." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/genesis/26.htm
- **Guzik:** "Wells were valuable, and they were difficult and expensive to dig. It was a significant attack to destroy someone's wells. This shows how strong the envy of the Philistines was towards Isaac." Isaac departed "peaceably and quietly" — a testimony to his non-confrontational character. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-26/
- **Bible.org:** "Digging a well was considered tantamount to a claim of ownership of the land on which it was located. It enabled a man to dwell there and to sustain herds. Rather than recognize this claim, the Philistines sought to wipe it out." — https://bible.org/seriespage/isaac-walks-his-father%E2%80%99s-steps-genesis-261-35

---

## vv. 18–19 — Reopening Abraham's Wells; A New Well of "Living Water"

**Traditional reading:** Isaac re-dug his father's wells and restored their original names, honouring Abraham's legacy. His servants then discovered a new well of "springing" (living/running) water — the best kind.

- **Guzik:** This is "a powerful illustration of life in the spirit. The spiritual resources that sustained previous generations are available for us today, if we will seek them with faith, work, and commitment." He adds: "the wells of peace, power, grace, wisdom, and transformation are available for the believer today as they were for previous generations." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-26/
- **Gill:** "Living water" that "continually flows, as Aben Ezra rightly interprets it: hence this phrase is used of the perpetual and ever living graces of the Spirit of God, John 4:10." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/26.htm
- **Bible.org:** Isaac found "living water" — "water that originated from a spring — running water, not simply water that was contained." — https://bible.org/seriespage/isaac-walks-his-father%E2%80%99s-steps-genesis-261-35

**Typological note:** Gill explicitly makes the Johannine connection to the Holy Spirit (John 4:10; 7:38), a reading common across traditions. This "living water" is seen as a type of the Spirit's perpetual, life-giving work.

---

## vv. 20–22 — Esek, Sitnah, and Rehoboth

**Traditional reading:** Three wells, three names. The herdsmen of Gerar quarrelled over the first two, so Isaac named them Esek ("contention") and Sitnah ("hostility/opposition," related to "Satan"). The third well was uncontested; Isaac named it Rehoboth ("broad places/room"), confessing God's provision.

- **Gill:** Esek = contention; Sitnah = hatred, "from this word Satan has his name, and these men were of a diabolical spirit, envious, spiteful, and malicious." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/26.htm
- **Guzik:** "Isaac saw these wells as they rightly were: the blessing of God. He saw them more as God's gracious blessing than the result of his hard work." God used the conflicts to lead Isaac back toward Beersheba. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-26/
- **Spurgeon (cited by Guzik):** "Like Isaac, after you have drunk of the waters of 'contention' and 'hatred', you will be brought to Rehoboth, where you shall have 'room', yea, even to Beer-sheba, 'the well of the oath' … where your enemies shall seek your favor, and glorify your Lord." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-26/

**Isaac's peaceful character:** Across traditions, Isaac's refusal to fight is praised. He moved on rather than wage war. This is seen as either meekness (commendable) or passivity (his natural timidity). The Reformed tradition especially sees this as evidence of his trust in God's sovereignty and timing. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/promise-isaac-part

---

## vv. 23–25 — At Beersheba: Altar, Worship, Tent, Well

**Traditional reading:** Isaac went up to Beersheba — the place associated with Abraham's covenant with Abimelech and where Abraham called on the LORD (Genesis 21:33). That night, God appeared and spoke: "I am the God of your father Abraham. Do not be afraid, for I am with you." Isaac responded by building an altar, worshipping, pitching his tent, and digging a well — in that order.

- **Bible.org** considers vv. 23–25 the interpretive key to the chapter: "Previously the touchstone for knowing the will of God had been circumstances … But now, having dug a well that was uncontested, we would have expected Isaac to dwell there. Instead … he moved on to Beersheba." The shift in the order of activities is crucial: altar first, then tent, then well. "The place for God's people is the place of God's presence … Material needs are thus considered last, while spiritual needs are primary." This is linked to Matthew 6:33. — https://bible.org/seriespage/isaac-walks-his-father%E2%80%99s-steps-genesis-261-35
- **Gill:** "The first night he came to Beersheba, in a dream or vision." God identifies Himself as the God of Abraham, who "though he was dead, he remembered the covenant he made with him." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/26.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "I (the pronoun is emphatic) am the God (the Elohim) of Abraham thy father … the language is expressive not alone of the covenant relationship which subsisted between Jehovah and the patriarch while the latter lived, but also of the present continuance of that relationship, since Abraham, though dead, had not ceased to be." The reason given — "for my servant Abraham's sake" — "declares God's gracious covenant, and not personal merit, to be the true source of blessing for Isaac." — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/26.htm
- **Guzik:** "God kept His covenant with Isaac for Abraham's sake. After the same pattern, God keeps His covenant with believers under the new covenant for the sake of Jesus Christ." Altars, tents, and wells marked Isaac's life just as they did Abraham's. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-26/

**Reformed (Ligonier/Calvin):** God's reassurance "do not fear" addresses Isaac's specific temptation to timidity. The blessing is "for my servant Abraham's sake" — rooted in God's gracious covenant, not Isaac's worthiness. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/promise-isaac-part

---

## vv. 26–31 — Covenant with Abimelech

**Traditional reading:** Abimelech travelled from Gerar with Ahuzzath (his advisor/councillor) and Phicol (his army commander) to make a treaty with Isaac. Isaac's blunt question — "Why have you come to me, since you hate me and have sent me away?" — reveals the tension. Abimelech's answer: "We can plainly see that the LORD has been with you … You are now blessed by the LORD." A feast and mutual oath follow.

- **Calvin:** "There is not the least doubt that the king was led to this measure, by a secret divine impulse." He notes it was remarkable that a king would humble himself to seek peace with a private man: "God had so forcibly impressed his mind, that he, forgetting his regal pride, sought for peace and alliance with a man who was neither covetous, nor warlike, nor furnished with a great army." — https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom02/calcom02.iv.i.html
- **Calvin on making covenants with unbelievers:** It is "lawful for the children of God to enter into league and friendship with heathen people who profess nothing but false religion — as long as we do not join ourselves with them, nor draw in the same yoke." — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/our-father-without-fault
- **JFB:** Abimelech and Phicol are "different persons' official titles" because ~90 years had passed since Abraham's treaty. The overture demonstrates the promise of Genesis 12:2 being fulfilled — God making Isaac's name great. Isaac's "timid and passive temper had submitted to the annoyances of his rude neighbors; but now … he evinces deep feeling at their conduct." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/genesis/26.htm
- **Guzik:** "Abimelech came to ask for peace and a blessing from Isaac … because he knew that God was with him." Isaac "didn't respond to evil by returning evil." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-26/
- **Pulpit Commentary** notes that Abimelech's claim to have done Isaac "nothing but good" (v. 29) was not strictly true — they had robbed him of two wells — but Isaac "does not press them any further." — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/26.htm

---

## vv. 32–33 — The Well Shibah and the Naming of Beersheba

**Traditional reading:** On the same day as the covenant feast, Isaac's servants reported finding water in a newly dug well. He named it Shibah ("oath" or "seven"), and the city retained the name Beersheba ("Well of the Oath" or "Well of Seven"). This parallels Abraham's naming of Beersheba in Genesis 21:31.

- **Guzik:** "God brought many good things to Isaac at once. He enjoyed a rich season of blessing." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-26/
- **Bible.org:** "The place where God wants us to be is also the place of provision … What was once Isaac's first concern was now his last, but water was still essential for his survival." — https://bible.org/seriespage/isaac-walks-his-father%E2%80%99s-steps-genesis-261-35

---

## vv. 34–35 — Esau's Hittite Wives

**Traditional reading:** At age forty, Esau married two Hittite women — Judith and Basemath — who brought "grief of mind" (literally "bitterness of spirit") to Isaac and Rebekah. This violated the Abrahamic pattern of not marrying Canaanite women (Genesis 24:3–4). These verses set the stage for the conflict of Genesis 27.

- **Gill:** The grief was "partly because they were Canaanites, being Hittites, with whom marriage was forbidden … and partly because they were idolatrous persons, and enticed Esau to idolatry." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/26.htm
- **JFB:** "These wives never gained the affections of his parents, and this estrangement was overruled by God for keeping the chosen family aloof from the dangers of heathen influence." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/genesis/26.htm
- **Guzik:** "Esau … went against the pattern established by Abraham … This was evidence of Esau's character as a fornicator and profane person (Hebrews 12:16)." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-26/
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The grief was "possibly because of their personal characters, but chiefly because of their Canaanitish descent, and because in marrying them Esau had not consulted his parents." — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/26.htm

**Note:** The BSB names differ from the KJV tradition. The wives are named Judith daughter of Beeri and Basemath daughter of Elon. (In Genesis 36:2–3, Esau's wives are named differently — Adah, Oholibamah, and Basemath daughter of Ishmael — a well-known textual difficulty. The traditional resolution: Esau had multiple wives, or different names were used at different times.)

---

## Points of Denominational Emphasis

**Reformed (Calvin, Ligonier):** Emphasises God's sovereign, unconditional election — the covenant passes to Isaac by God's gracious choice, not Isaac's merit. Abraham's obedience (v. 5) is the fruit of justifying faith. Isaac's passivity and timidity are weaknesses, but God's faithfulness overcomes them. The covenant with Abimelech demonstrates God's providence over pagan rulers. — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/promise-isaac-part ; https://ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom02/calcom02.iv.i.html

**Baptist (Gill, Spurgeon):** Gill's commentary is thorough on the Hebrew text and historical details. Spurgeon (cited by Guzik) draws spiritual typology from the wells: the believer moves through contention and hatred before reaching enlargement and rest. Emphasis on personal faith and obedience following Abraham's pattern. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/26.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-26/

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Emphasises the spiritual lessons from the wells — that the resources of previous generations (peace, power, grace, wisdom) are available today if believers pursue them with "faith, work, and commitment." The "living water" well is connected to the Holy Spirit's ongoing work. Practical application to "spiritual warfare" through the contention wells. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-26/

**Lutheran (LCMS):** While no specifically Lutheran Genesis 26 commentary was retrieved in searches, Lutheran teaching would emphasise that the covenant promises come by grace alone, that Isaac (like all believers) is simultaneously sinner and saint (his deception alongside his faith), and that God's Word of promise creates and sustains faith.

**Methodist/Wesleyan:** The emphasis on Abraham's obedience (v. 5) as pattern for covenant faithfulness resonates with Wesleyan themes of holy living as the proper response to grace. The centering of life on the altar (v. 25) before material concerns models the priority of worship and devotion.

**Catholic (traditional):** The Catholic tradition reads this chapter as part of salvation history, with Isaac as a type of Christ (the beloved son, the bridegroom, the well-digger who gives living water). Abraham's obedience (v. 5) illustrates that faith works through love (cf. Galatians 5:6), consistent with Catholic teaching on faith and works.

---

## Key Themes Across All Traditions

1. **Covenant faithfulness:** God keeps His promises across generations.
2. **The repeated pattern of sin:** Isaac repeats Abraham's failure — a sobering warning.
3. **God's protection despite human weakness:** God preserves Isaac and Rebekah even when Isaac's faith falters.
4. **Peaceful response to opposition:** Isaac's non-retaliation is commended.
5. **The priority of worship:** Building the altar before digging the well (v. 25) models seeking God's kingdom first.
